title: Exploring the role and mechanism of methionine metabolism in chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps based on bioinformatics analysis.
authors: Lin, Dan
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps (CRSwNP) affects 1%-4% of the global population with high recurrence rates. While methionine metabolism abnormalities contribute to various inflammatory diseases, their role in CRSwNP pathogenesis remains unclear. This study aimed to systematically investigate the role of methionine metabolism in CRSwNP and identify potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets through integrating multi-omics data and interpretable machine learning approaches. METHODS: CRSwNP transcriptomic datasets (GSE136825, GSE179265) and single-cell data (GSE276503) were obtained from GEO database. Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis, differential expression analysis using limma, and Weighted Gene co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) were performed to identify methionine metabolism-related candidate genes. Three machine learning algorithms (LASSO, SVM-RFE, XGBoost) with SHAP interpretation screened core genes. Functions and mechanisms were explored through single-gene GSEA, ceRNA network construction, transcription factor prediction, immune infiltration analysis, and pseudotime trajectory analysis. Potential therapeutic drugs were identified via molecular docking. RESULTS: Among 14 candidate genes, CSTB, IGFBP3, and TCN1 were identified as core genes with excellent diagnostic performance (AUC > 0.85). SHAP analysis revealed CSTB and IGFBP3 as disease risk-promoting factors, while TCN1 showed protective effects. Single-cell analysis demonstrated all three genes were predominantly expressed in epithelial cells with significant differential expression patterns. They were enriched in primary immunodeficiency pathways and significantly correlated with immune cell infiltration, particularly M2 macrophages and activated dendritic cells. Molecular docking identified five potential therapeutic drugs including ambroxol, carbamazepine, and curcumin with favorable binding energies. CONCLUSION: Methionine metabolism participates in CRSwNP pathogenesis by regulating CSTB, IGFBP3, and TCN1, affecting epithelial cell function and immune microenvironment. These genes represent promising biomarkers for diagnosis and potential therapeutic targets, providing theoretical basis for developing metabolic-immune intervention strategies in CRSwNP management.

title: pH/GSH-responsive dual chitosan/PLA-coated cobalt ferrite nanoparticles for targeted and selective quinidine delivery in hepatocellular carcinoma.
authors: Anter, Esraa; Elshami, Fawzya I; Shereef, Hadeer A; Abdou, Safaa N; van Eldik, Rudi; Shaban, Shaban Y
abstract: Drug repurposing using smart nanocarriers may help overcome chemoresistance and poor tumor selectivity in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Here, a pH/GSH-responsive dual chitosan/polylactic acid coated cobalt ferrite nanoparticle system (QL-CS/PLA-CFO NPs) has been explored to deliver QL for treating HCC. QL-CS/PLA-CFO NPs were prepared via ionotropic gelation and w/o/w emulsion with high loading (64.8%) and excellent stability (+28.0 mV). Comparative formulations, chitosan-only QL-CS-CFO (50.9%, -10.5 mV) and nonmagnetic QL-CS/PLA (60.7%, -21.0 mV), elucidated the roles of coating architecture and magnetic core. QL-CS/PLA-CFO NPs released 10.8% at pH 7.4 versus  approximately 95% at pH 4.5 with 10 mM GSH over 180 h, following quasi-Fickian diffusion kinetics. Encapsulation increased the WI38/HepG2 IC(5)(0) ratio from 1.12 to 1.93 through controlled endosomal release and protecting normal cells, with  approximately 1.2% hemolysis and enhanced DPPH antioxidants IC(5)(0) (47.9 vs. 71.9 mug/mL for free QL). DNA-binding studies revealed PLA-CFO synergy, yielding 38-fold enhanced affinity versus free QL through a minor-groove binding mode. Molecular docking suggested a potential interaction between quinidine and the HCC-associated biomarker glypican-3 (PDB 3GJB), supporting future investigation of its biological relevance. QL-CS/PLA-CFO NPs represent a promising platform for selective QL delivery in HCC, warranting further in vivo evaluation.

title: Mitochondrial Metabolism-Related Candidate Signatures in Calcific Aortic Valve Disease Spectrum: An Exploratory Integrative Bioinformatics Study.
authors: Yang, Min; Gui, Yingjing; Qian, Hongbo; Zhang, Dafa
abstract: ​Calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) is a progressive valvular disorder in which the role of mitochondrial metabolism remains incompletely understood. This exploratory study aimed to identify mitochondrial metabolism-related genes (MIMMRGs) associated with CAVD-spectrum valve remodeling. GSE83453 was used as the training dataset, and GSE51472 was used for expression-direction validation. Both datasets contain biologically and phenotypically heterogeneous groups of diseased valves. CAVD-associated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were integrated with MIMMRGs, followed by functional enrichment analysis, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), and support vector machine-recursive feature elimination (SVM-RFE), expression validation, immune infiltration analysis, transcription factor analysis, drug and compound prediction, and molecular docking. A total of 909 DEGs and 1,234 MIMMRGs were identified, yielding 67 candidate genes enriched in metabolic and biosynthetic processes. ACADL and TDO2 were identified as candidate biomarkers and exhibited consistent expression differences between CAVD and normal samples in both datasets. Gene set enrichment analysis indicated the involvement of chemokine-related and immune-regulatory pathways. Four immune cell types differed between the CAVD and normal groups, and ACADL and TDO2 exhibited opposite correlations with naive B cells. HNF4A, STAT3, and AR were predicted to be common transcriptional regulators. Molecular docking indicated favorable in silico interactions between doxorubicin and ACADL and between dexamethasone and TDO2. In conclusion, ACADL and TDO2 are candidate biomarkers associated with mitochondrial metabolism and immune-related processes in heterogeneous CAVD-spectrum valve lesions. These findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating and require independent clinical and experimental validation.

title: Yixintai granules enhance glucose and lipid metabolism after ischemic heart failure by regulating inflammatory factors via the LPS/TLR4/NF-kappaB signaling pathway.
authors: Wang, Ziyan; Liu, Chengxin; Wei, Jiaming; Mao, Yiwen; Yuan, Hui; Shi, Min; Lin, Ruifang; Ding, Zehui; Zhou, Yinli; Guo, Zhihua; Ge, Jinwen; Long, Yun; Li, Ya
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ischemic heart failure (IHF) severely impacts patients' quality of life and leads to frequent hospitalizations, increased healthcare costs, and increased mortality rates, thus posing a substantial global health challenge. Myocardial ischemia is a primary trigger of HF. Yixintai granules (YXT), a traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formulation, have demonstrated clinical benefits in HF treatment; however, their underlying mechanisms remain unclear. METHODS: The components of YXT absorbed into the blood were identified using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS). The key regulatory mechanisms underlying its therapeutic effects on HF were clarified using network pharmacology, and the binding affinity of key YXT components to proteins associated with the LPS/TLR4/NF-kappaB pathway was assessed through molecular docking. In vivo experiments involved the establishment of an HF rat model through the ligation of the left anterior descending coronary artery. In vitro experiments utilized an H9C2 cell injury model induced by lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which was subsequently treated with YXT-containing serum. RESULTS: UHPLC-MS/MS analysis identified 2,581 active components in the YXT and 1,055 active components in the YXT-containing serum. Network pharmacology indicated that the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines mediated by the LPS/TLR4/NF-kappaB pathway and glucolipid metabolic disorders may significantly contribute to the anti-HF effects of YXT. Subsequent in vivo experiments revealed that YXT enhanced cardiac function, reduced myocardial fibrosis, and improved mitochondrial morphology in HF rats. Additionally, it lowered inflammatory cytokine levels and was associated with altered glucose and lipid metabolic profiles and inhibition of the LPS/TLR4/NF-kappaB signaling pathway. In vitro experiments revealed that YXT-containing serum alleviated LPS-induced H9c2 cardiac cell injury, reduced reactive oxygen species and inflammatory cytokine levels, and was associated with altered glucose and lipid metabolic profiles and inhibition of the LPS/TLR4/NF-kappaB signaling pathway. CONCLUSION: YXT improved cardiac function and attenuated fibrosis and ultrastructural damage in IHF rats, with effects associated with LPS/TLR4/NF-kappaB signaling inhibition, reduced inflammation, and altered glucose/lipid metabolic profiles.

title: Icariin and kartogenin: research on the mechanism of combined intervention on chondrogenic differentiation of BMSCs via the Wnt/beta‑catenin pathway.
authors: Xiang, Wei; Yu, Xia; Chen, Rui; Feng, Huirong; Zhang, Lei; Song, Chao; Wu, Jiaqi; Chen, Xiaojun
abstract: BACKGROUND: Although additional research is needed to identify the exact molecular mechanisms, studies have demonstrated that icariin (ICA) and kartogenin (KGN) can promote bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells to develop chondrogenically. METHODS: Employ SwissTarget prediction and PUBCHEM to ascertain the chemical composition and expected targets of KGN and ICA. OA chip data should be gathered for a bioinformatics investigation using the GEO database. To find targets associated with the disease, use "osteoarthritis" as a search criterion in the GeneCards database. Using chip and GeneCard data, determine which ICA and KGN targets overlap, then build core genes. Next, conduct KEGG and GO enrichment analyses. Use molecular docking to verify the hub genes' and essential components' binding activity. Alcian blue staining, QPCR, and western blot were used to identify the effects of ICA and KGN intervention on mouse BMSCs. RESULTS: The bioinformatics investigation of ICA and KGN treatment for OA revealed six possible therapeutic gene targets, primarily HSP90AA1 SOX9 COL2A1 ACAN GSK3B CTNNB1. Based on target enrichment research, ICA and KGN's biological effects in treating OA appear to be mostly associated with skeletal system development, positive control of protein degradation, chondrocyte differentiation, and negative regulation of the normal Wnt signaling pathway. According to KEGG enrichment analysis, the primary pathways impacted were the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, the Wnt signaling, the ErbB signaling pathway, cell cycle, the mTOR signaling pathway, and necroptosis. Of these, the Wnt signaling pathway is crucial. CONCLUSION: According to this study, the combined intervention of ICA and KGN may be associated with the Wnt/beta‑catenin pathway to regulate chondrogenic differentiation of mouse BMSCs, providing new insights for OA treatment research.

title: Cross-task benchmarking reveals variable transferability of deep learning models across molecular quantitative trait loci.
authors: Chen, Sihan; Wang, Xiaoyu; Peleg, Anton Y; Xu, Shuting; Li, Fuyi; Webb, Geoffrey I; Song, Jiangning
abstract: Most genetic variants associated with complex traits reside in non-coding regions of the genome, complicating their functional interpretation. Recent deep learning models have advanced the prediction of expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs), but whether these models generalize across diverse molecular phenotypes is unknown. Here, we assess the cross-task transferability of pretrained regulatory features from six representative sequence- and annotation-based models across nine classes of molecular quantitative trait loci (xQTLs). We observe that while all models perform well in eQTL prediction, their performance varies substantially across other xQTL predictions. Chromatin accessibility, transcription factor binding, and histone QTLs are generally well predicted, whereas chromatin looping and microRNA expression QTLs remain challenging. Foundation models, particularly AlphaGenome and Borzoi, consistently outperform models based on local sequence context and exhibit improved robustness across class-imbalance settings. Tree-based ensemble classifiers further enhance predictive performance, suggesting that nonlinear interactions among regulatory features contribute substantially to variant prioritization. Applying AlphaGenome and Borzoi to coronary artery disease-associated genome-wide association studies loci identifies 337 high-confidence candidate chromatin accessibility QTLs, including 11 previously reported and 326 candidates that display significantly larger allele-specific differences in predicted chromatin accessibility signals. Collectively, our results reveal substantial variability in the cross-task performance of current eQTL-centric models, highlight the advantages of long-range genomic representations and inform the prioritization of candidate regulatory variants contributing to complex diseases.

title: Towards precision medicine in diabetes: pharmacogenomic approaches for MODY and type 2 diabetes with insights from GLIS3 gene variants.
authors: Lenin, Abhisheka; Sajini Rajayan, Jasmin
abstract: BACKGROUND: Diabetes mellitus encompasses a heterogeneous group of metabolic disorders with a significant genetic basis that current standardized treatment protocols fail to adequately address. Type 2 diabetes in particular is driven by genetic factors that operate independently of lifestyle, with a substantial proportion of patients in South Asian populations developing the disease despite normal body weight and healthy habits. India presents a uniquely important context for pharmacogenomic research given its extraordinary population stratification across tribal, linguistic, religious, and geographic groups creating a genetic landscape that Western genomic data cannot adequately represent. OBJECTIVE: This review evaluates pharmacogenomic evidence across monogenic and polygenic diabetes subtypes, presents Indian clinical case studies demonstrating the consequences of genomic misclassification, and positions GLIS3 as an underexplored regulatory gene with cross-disease relevance spanning neonatal diabetes, Type 1, and Type 2 diabetes. It further examines the potential for expanded clinical implementation of genotype-guided therapy, particularly in genetically diverse populations. KEY INSIGHTS: GLIS3 encodes a zinc finger transcription factor that governs beta-cell development, insulin gene transcription, and endoplasmic reticulum stress protection by functioning as a master regulator of beta-cell survival rather than acting through a single pathway. Its association across multiple diabetes subtypes, combined with emerging evidence of population-specific variants in Indian cohorts, positions it as a compelling future pharmacogenomic target. However, no GLIS3-directed clinical testing or therapy is currently available, and its pharmacogenomic utility remains hypothetical pending prospective validation. Indian pharmacogenomic data further reveal 76 known variants affecting antidiabetic drug response, with higher frequencies of poor metformin response alleles compared to global population findings with immediate clinical implications for one of the world's highest diabetes-burden nations. CONCLUSION: Realizing the potential of precision medicine in diabetes requires population-specific genomic research, integration of pharmacogenomic testing into national health schemes such as Ayushman Bharat, development of AI-driven clinical decision tools, and policy frameworks guided by bodies such as ICMR. Genotype-guided therapy represents an emerging clinical priority with the potential to improve outcomes in genetically diverse populations where standardized protocols may be suboptimal.

title: Jianpi Huayu decoction induces hepatocellular carcinoma apoptosis through flavonoid components targeting tumor protein p53 activation and serine-threonine protein kinase 1/B-cell lymphoma 2 inhibition: a network pharmacology-based study with experimental validation.
authors: Xiaokai, Chen; Yingjie, Xie; Hui, W U; Yong, L I; Yantong, L U; Wei, Tan; Changjun, Wang; Xuhui, Huang
journal: Journal of traditional Chinese medicine = Chung i tsa chih ying wen pan
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To investigate the bioactive components and molecular mechanisms by which Jianpi Huayu decoction (, JHD) promotes apoptosis in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). METHODS: A multi-omics strategy integrating serum pharmacochemistry, metabolomics, network analysis, molecular docking, and in vitro validation was employed. Serum-absorbed components were identified from JHD-treated rats. Core targets and pathways were analyzed viaprotein-protein interaction (PPI) networks and kyoto encyclopedia of genes and genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment. The effects of key candidate components (apigenin, naringin, daidzein, curzerenone, curcumenol) were validated in human hepatoma G2 cell line cells through cell viability, apoptosis, and protein expression assays. RESULTS: Fifty-one serum-absorbed JHD compounds were identified, comprising eight alkaloids, fifteen flavonoids, nine terpenoids, three quinones, and three phenylpropanoids. Apigenin, naringin, and daidzein demonstrated the highest bioavailability. Network analysis identified tumor protein 53 (TP53), serine-threonine kinase 1 (AKT1), B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL2), epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), and Jun proto-oncogene (JUN) as core targets, which converge on major cancer-related pathways, including phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)-serine-threonine kinase (AKT), mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK), and Janus kinase (JAK)-signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3). Molecular docking revealed stable binding of naringin to AKT1 [binding energy: －12.6 kcal/mol; root mean square deviation (RMSD): 0.2-0.4 nm]. Apigenin showed the strongest binding affinity for TP53 (－8.2 kcal/mol) and AKT1 (－9.6 kcal/mol). In vitro, apigenin [half maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) = 48.2 muM at 24 h] significantly upregulated TP53 (P < 0.01) while downregulating BCL2 (P < 0.05), AKT1 (P < 0.01), JUN (P < 0.0001), and EGFR (P < 0.01). Both naringin and curzerenone downregulated AKT1 and BCL2 at 48 h (P < 0.05). In contrast, curcumenol (a structural analog of curzerenone) exhibited no significant regulatory effects (P > 0.05). CONCLUSION: JHD promotes HCC apoptosis primarily viaits flavonoid-enriched components, notably apigenin and naringin, which function by activating TP53 and inhibiting the AKT1/BCL2 signaling axis. This study establishes a "component-target-pathway" framework for optimizing herbal formulations and bridges Traditional Chinese Medicine with precision oncology for flavonoid-based HCC therapy.

title: Computational prioritization and molecular dynamics analysis of FOXA2 missense variants with potential relevance to colorectal cancer.
authors: Mia, Md Sohel; Talukder, Md Enamul Kabir; Tanmoy, Md Shahed Imam; Raisa, Israt Jahan; Datta, Bimal Kumar; Shadhin, Md Saklain Tanver; Tahsin, Nowmee; Imon, Raihan Rahman; Aktaruzzaman, Md; Zargar, Seema; Wani, Tanveer A
abstract: The pioneer transcription factor FOXA2 controls developmental gene programmes, metabolic homeostasis and epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity, and its expression dysregulation is a recognized feature of colorectal cancer. The structural and thermodynamic consequences of FOXA2 missense variants remain poorly defined. We interrogated 659 missense SNPs across the human FOXA2 locus within an integrated multi-algorithm framework. Sequential filtering with SIFT, PolyPhen-2, PhD-SNP and SNPs&GO converged on three high-confidence deleterious variants (M190I, R197Q and L402P), which were profiled further with ConSurf, I-Mutant 2.0, MUpro, MutPred2 and DynaMut2. Conservation and structural mapping placed M190I (ConSurf-8) and R197Q (ConSurf-9) in the winged-helix DNA-binding domain (PF00250) and L402P (ConSurf-5) in the HNF_C domain (PF09354). R197Q is solvent-exposed and predicted to perturb promoter DNA contacts, whereas the buried M190I and L402P substitutions are predicted to act through local destabilization at the substitution site. In three independent 50-ns molecular dynamics replicates per system, all variants deviated from wild-type backbone behavior. M190I converged prematurely into a displaced conformational state, whereas R197Q and L402P continued to drift late in the trajectories. Backbone fluctuations increased non-locally, clustering in flexible regulatory segments (~290-316) and the C-terminal transactivation domain 2 (452-456). Principal component analysis indicated a more concentrated collective-mode structure in the mutants, and dynamic cross-correlation analysis weakened residue coupling, consistent with disrupted long-range communication. Of twelve trajectory-level comparisons, only the R197Q hydrogen-bond reduction reached nominal significance (p = 0.025, Hedges' g = -2.28), indicating a large reduction in average hydrogen-bond count relative to wild-type; the remaining eleven comparisons showed non-significant moderate-to-large effects. Expression enrichment was highest in colorectal cancer cell lines, providing expression-level context for FOXA2 in CRC biology. These findings computationally prioritize M190I, R197Q and L402P as candidates for experimental validation.

title: Salt-Mediated Long-Range Electrostatic Signature of Native Binding Surface Pre-Organizes Bound-Like Conformations of p53 C-Terminal Intrinsically Disordered Region.
authors: Das, Kingshuk; Jana, Biman
journal: Chemphyschem : a European journal of chemical physics and physical chemistry
abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and regions (IDRs) often undergo a disorder-to-order transition via coupled folding and binding. The p53 C-terminal domain (CTD) IDR folds into a helical conformation upon binding S100B, yet the long-range influence of the ionic environment on this transition remains poorly understood. Using all-atom molecular dynamics simulations with a novel confinement setup, we investigated the conformational landscape of a 12-residue fragment of p53 CTD at varying distances from the S100B binding cleft. Comparing behavior in pure water and physiological salt (150 mM NaCl), we find that at 10 A from the native binding surface, the peptide spontaneously forms stable, bound-like helical segments exclusively in the salt solution. This effect is distance-dependent, vanishing at 20 A, and specific to the native binding surface, notably occurring without direct protein-IDR contacts. Our results demonstrate that the negatively charged S100B surface organizes solvated ions into a structured, long-range electrostatic microenvironment that thermodynamically stabilizes bound-like helical conformations prior to direct contact. This reveals a synergistic effect between native surface topology and physiological salt that biases the IDR's conformational ensemble to facilitate binding, identifying the ions in the solution as active participants in molecular recognition.

title: Evolutionary origin of the WHIRLY gene families across 330 plant species: from algae to land plants.
authors: Lan, Yanhong; Gong, Fangyi; Dong, Rongjiang; Fang, Chao; Cai, Peng
abstract: Phylogenomics of 921 WHIRLY genes across 330 plants reveals stepwise subfamily origins, purifying selection, and a novel AtWHY1/2/3 hetero-oligomeric stress complex. Whirly (WHY) transcription factors are a plant-specific, highly conserved family with central roles in organellar genome maintenance, retrograde signaling, and abiotic stress response, but their deep evolutionary trajectories across the full green plant lineage have remained largely unresolved. In the present study, 921 WHY genes were identified across 330 different species from algae to land plants, which were classified into three subfamilies (WHY I, WHY II, and WHY III) in this study. Structural characteristics of different subfamilies showed significant differences in the number of exons and protein motifs, which may have arisen due to functional differentiation. Collinearity was primarily observed among members of the same subfamily, and network clustering analysis further divided all WHY genes into three clusters, with genes within each cluster exhibiting significant collinearity. All three subfamilies are under intense long-term purifying selection, with average Ka/Ks ratios far below 1, indicating stringent evolutionary constraints on their core conserved single-stranded DNA binding domain. Using yeast two-hybrid assays, protein molecular docking and site-specific interaction validation, we further uncovered a previously unreported stable hetero-oligomeric complex formed by AtWHY1, AtWHY2, and AtWHY3, assembled via defined hydrogen bond networks and salt bridges at the conserved interface residues, which acts as a combinatorial regulatory switch to coordinate distinct subcellular stress responses. This work establishes a unified evolutionary framework for the WHY family and provides new mechanistic insights into how their hetero-oligomerization drives specialized stress adaptation during plant territorialization.

title: Prediction of Residue-Level Base Preference for DNA-Binding Proteins Using a Multimodal Learning Framework.
authors: Li, Siyuan; He, Wenyan; Zhang, Mengru; Zhang, Xin; Fang, Wei-Qun; Xu, Min-Juan; Shi, Yi; Cai, Yujia; Zhang, Yong; Da, Lin-Tai
abstract: Specific recognition between proteins and DNA governs essential cellular functions, yet the binding specificity of most DNA-binding proteins (DBPs) remains experimentally uncharacterized and high-throughput experimental methods still lag far behind the ever-growing protein data set. Here, we present 3M-BSIP (3-modal base-specific interaction predictor), a multimodal deep learning framework capable of predicting the DNA-binding interface and residue-level base preference for DBPs. 3M-BSIP constructs a holistic protein representation by integrating three distinct modalities: a protein language model capturing evolutionary conservation; a graph neural network encoding 3D structural features; and a hierarchical encoder characterizing physicochemical properties of protein surface pointclouds. Comprehensive benchmarking demonstrates that 3M-BSIP achieves SOTA performance on both interface-residue identification and base-preference predictions. Crucially, the model maintains robust performance on computationally constructed protein structures and is also tolerant toward those undergoing profound structural rearrangements upon DNA binding. Two real-world applications of 3M-BSIP demonstrate that our model not only can accurately predict the specific binding motif of structurally unknown transcription factors but also, more importantly, can guide rapid reprogramming of the base preference of DBPs based on a purely computational pipeline. Therefore, 3M-BSIP holds great potential in annotating the binding motifs of all DBPs in a high-throughput manner and designing new DBPs with desired base specificities.

title: Identification of ageing-related genes in prostate cancer with type 2 Diabetes using machine learning: a multi-omics study focusing on SOX4, PRNP, and FOXO4.
authors: Zhang, Wei; Zhang, Xueqian; Zhang, Chenghao; Shi, Xinyang; Deng, Yiheng; Gao, Yan; Bi, Kaipeng; Wang, Zheng; Chen, Guanqiu; Ye, Zhoujie; An, Ziyan; Fu, Weijun
abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) demonstrates complex associations with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and ageing, though their interconnected molecular mechanisms remain poorly defined. This study aimed to identify and validate diagnostic biomarkers at the intersection of these pathways to enable early detection and risk stratification in high-risk populations. Bioinformatic analysis was performed on PCa and T2DM transcriptomic data downloaded from the GEO database, followed by differential expression analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), and functional enrichment. Eight machine learning algorithms were applied to identify hub ageing-related genes (ARGs), with SHAP analysis interpreting feature importance. A nomogram model was constructed and validated across multiple cohorts. Immune infiltration, drug sensitivity, single-cell RNA sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics were used for mechanistic exploration. Three key ARGs (SOX4, PRNP, and FOXO4) were identified and used to develop a diagnostic model with high accuracy (AUCs: 0.726-0.905). SOX4 promoted immune evasion, PRNP exhibited context-dependent duality, and FOXO4 functioned as a tumor suppressor. Spatial and single-cell analyses revealed cell-type-specific expression and fibroblast-epithelial communication via MIF, LRP1, and FZD1. Drug sensitivity profiling identified abiraterone and docetaxel as potential therapeutics for high- and low-risk patients, respectively. In conclusion, SOX4, PRNP, and FOXO4 are key biomarkers linking PCa, T2DM, and ageing, and the diagnostic model shows robust performance and clinical utility, providing insights into microenvironment-driven mechanisms and personalized treatment strategies for PCa patients with T2DM.

title: Genetic variants shape single-cell chromatin accessibility and disease risk.
authors: Xue, Angli; Fan, Jianan; Dong, Oscar A; Huang, Hao Lawrence; Chen, Ling; Allen, Peter C; Spenceley, Eleanor; Sagi-Zsigmond, Eszter; Bowen, Blake; Henry, Albert; Cuomo, Anna S E; Tanudisastro, Hope A; Qiao, Zhen; Dorans, Elizabeth; Ben-David, Eyal; Farh, Kyle Kai-How; Hu, Linfeng; Liu, Yijia Christiana; Neavin, Drew R; Lee, Arthur S; Senabouth, Anne; Bartie, Caitlin; McCloy, Rachael A; Chin, Venessa; Zhou, Wei; Price, Alkes L; de Lange, Katrina M; Figtree, Gemma A; Hewitt, Alex W; MacArthur, Daniel G; Powell, Joseph E
abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation at single-cell resolution is crucial for elucidating complex disease mechanisms(1), but has been limited by the lack of large-scale single-cell multi-omics data(2-4). Here we present single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing of 3.5 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 1,042 donors with matched whole-genome sequencing. Across 28 immune cell types, we tested 440,996 chromatin accessibility peaks and identified 243,225 chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTLs) at 100,483 peaks, 60% of them cell-type specific. Rare variant analysis identified 38,161 associated peaks, with predicted transcription factor-binding disruption implicated at individual loci. Colocalization with expression QTLs (eQTLs) from single-cell RNA sequencing data (5.4 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells)(5) defined 28,834 candidate cis-regulatory elements. Across genome-wide association studies for 16 diseases and 44 blood traits, caQTLs colocalized 4.5-22.6% more signals than eQTLs alone. Cell-type-specific and tissue-specific context, distal effects and multi-causal-variant models raised genome-wide association study-eQTL concordance from approximately 16% to approximately 65%. Cell state further modulates genetic effects, with 27% of over 200,000 caQTL-cell-state interactions lacking a main effect. At the inflammatory bowel disease risk gene ADCY7, accessibility effects varied with genotype and G protein-mediated pathway activity in CD4(+) T cells. A graph neural network trained on both eQTL and caQTL layers inferred peak-gene links in unpaired multiome data with up to 17.2% higher accuracy than QTL-agnostic data, uncovering 128 additional transcription factor-target pairs (22% increase). Together, these results show that genetic variants shape chromatin accessibility in a cell-type-specific and cell-state-specific manner, influencing immune function and disease risk.

title: Spatiotemporal Multi-Omics Reveals Primate-Specific Mechanisms of Liver Regeneration Following Partial Hepatectomy.
authors: Feng, Guihai; Wang, Xin; Li, Pengcheng; Wang, Yang; Wan, Haifeng; Dong, Kangning; Deng, Haohao; Zou, Yu; Hu, Yilong; Jiang, Shuyang; Zhang, Runxue; Li, Fan; Wang, Siqi; Ding, Yali; Wang, Shuai; Zhang, Jing; Chen, Xingming; Gao, Jiao; He, Feng; Liu, Xuelai; Zhang, Ying; Gao, Jie; Xu, Cheng-Ran; Zhang, Shihua; Zhou, Qi; Li, Xin; Li, Wei
abstract: BACKGROUND & AIMS: The liver is a vital metabolic organ with an extraordinary capacity for regeneration, making it a key focus for understanding tissue repair and developing therapeutic strategies for liver diseases. However, ethical limitations restrict liver regeneration research largely to rodents, leaving critical gaps in our understanding of primate-specific mechanisms. METHODS: We performed partial hepatectomy (PHx) using a novel laparoscopically assisted hepatic wedge resection (LAHWR) approach in two cynomolgus monkeys (Macaca fascicularis), one for mechanistic exploration and one for validation. Afterwards, we performed sequential sampling and applied integrative multi-omics approaches, including snRNA-Seq, snATAC-Seq, and spatial transcriptomics (Stereo-Seq), to systematically map cellular and molecular dynamics of primate liver regeneration. RESULTS: We successfully established two non-human primate models to study the spatiotemporal dynamics of liver regeneration following PHx. We generate a high-resolution map of cellular and molecular dynamics of primate liver regeneration. Our analysis identified a distinct hepatocyte subcluster with fetal liver-like transcriptional features and high regenerative activity emerging in the early stages post-PHx (18.83% in Day 3 vs. 0.48% in Day 0), which predominantly localizes in midlobular zone 2 (P < 0.0001). This subcluster was characterized by elevated expression of proliferation-associated genes and was regulated by key transcription factor POU2F1. Cross-species comparisons revealed that POU2F1 is a primate-specific regulator of liver regeneration, showing significant upregulation in primates (P < 0.01), but not in rodents. Importantly, POU2F1 expression was markedly upregulated in cirrhotic patients (2 for liver samples). CONCLUSION: Proliferative hepatocytes localize primarily to midlobular zone 2 during primate hepatectomy regeneration process. POU2F1 is a primate-specific regulator of liver regeneration, implying novel regulatory mechanisms and emphasizing species-specific features. IMPACT AND IMPLICATIONS: The specific mechanisms of liver regeneration in primates remain poorly understood. The hepatocyte population expressing POU2F1 is a hepatocyte cluster with high proliferative capacity, induced after PHx, mainly located in zone 2 of liver lobule. Comparative studies of liver regeneration across species indicate that POU2F1 is a specific regulator in the liver regeneration process of primates. The therapeutic targeting of POU2F1+ hepatocytes is of potential interest in human liver regeneration.

title: XChrom: A Cross-Cell Chromatin Accessibility Prediction Model Integrating Genomic Sequence and Cellular Context.
authors: Miao, Yuanyuan; Liang, Xuan; Zhang, Wenwen; Han, Dongmei; Li, Yurun; Wang, Zhen
abstract: Single-cell chromatin accessibility offers unique insights into transcriptional regulation beyond gene expression. However, paired datasets of these two modalities remain relatively scarce, and existing computational models cannot simultaneously predict chromatin accessibility for unseen genomic regions and cells. Here, we present XChrom, a deep learning framework for genome-wide cross-cell chromatin accessibility prediction that integrates genomic sequence and single-cell transcriptomics-derived cell identity into a unified model. Comprehensive evaluations show that XChrom consistently outperforms existing methods in cross-region and cross-cell predictions, and uniquely enables cross-both predictions. It also supports cross-sample prediction when batch effects are properly corrected. Cross-species analyses demonstrate XChrom's robust performance and its ability to capture evolutionarily conserved regulatory rules. Applied to peripheral blood mononuclear cells from COVID-19 patients, XChrom accurately identifies transcription factor activities in novel but related cell states and reveals pathogenesis-associated regulatory alterations. XChrom is available as an open-source Python package, facilitating single-cell transcriptional regulation research.

title: Identification and validation of candidate biomarkers associated with mitochondrial metabolism in diabetic foot.
authors: Li, Haifeng; Ning, Yijie; Lu, Chuanlong; Zhang, Yuhang; Yan, Sheng; Chang, Wenkai; Jin, Haijiang; Tian, Qinqin; Shi, Yongbin; Qiao, Maolin; Zhang, Yudan; Dong, Honglin
abstract: BACKGROUND: Although the precise regulatory mechanisms underlying diabetic foot (DF) remain incompletely understood, increasing evidence suggests that mitochondrial metabolism may be involved in DF progression. The study aimed to identify and validate candidate biomarkers associated with mitochondrial metabolism in DF. METHODS: Transcriptome sequencing data from 12 DF and 18 control tissue samples were analyzed together with 1,234 mitochondrial metabolism-related genes (MMRGs), which were obtained from MSigDB by integrating curated gene sets directly associated with mitochondrial metabolic processes. First, overlapping genes between MMRGs and DEGs between DF and control samples were used as candidate genes. Then, candidate biomarkers were identified using PPI network construction, two machine learning algorithms, and ROC curve analysis. Next, based on the candidate biomarkers, functional enrichment, immune infiltration, regulatory network, compound prediction, as well as molecular docking analyses were undertaken. Finally, to explore the expression of candidate biomarkers in clinical samples, the reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) was performed. RESULTS: GPAT3 and PTGS2 were identified as mitochondrial metabolism-associated candidate biomarkers for DF, with area under the curve values of 0.963 and 0.958, respectively. Functional enrichment analysis showed that multiple pathways were significantly enriched by both GPAT3 and PTGS2, such as ribosome and Leishmania infection. GPAT3 had the strongest positive and negative correlations with neutrophils and resting CD4 memory T cells, respectively. In contrast, PTGS2 exhibited the strongest negative connection with M1 macrophages and the strongest positive correlation with neutrophils. Subsequently, multiple transcription factors (TFs) were found to co-target GPAT3 and PTGS2, such as BRD4 and NR0B1. Moreover, compound prediction analysis identified several compounds potentially associated with these biomarkers, such as lipopolysaccharides and cisplatin. The binding free energy between PTGS2 and tetradecanoylphorbol acetate was - 8.2 kcal/mol, while the binding free energy between GPAT3 and cyclosporine was - 10.4 kcal/mol, according to molecular docking data. Finally, the expression levels of GPAT3 and PTGS2 were significantly different in clinical samples. CONCLUSION: GPAT3 and PTGS2 were identified as candidate biomarkers associated with mitochondrial metabolism in DF, providing molecular clues for further investigation of DF pathogenesis and potential intervention strategies.

title: Desoxo-narchinol A and water extract of Nardostachys jatamansi ameliorate house dust mite-induced atopic dermatitis by regulating Nrf2/HO-1 signaling.
authors: Shim, Ki-Shuk; Kim, Hye Jin; Baek, Su-Jin; Gu, Dong Ryun; Kim, Yu Jin; Kim, Seong Cheol; Chae, Sungwook; Kim, Taesoo; Kim, Ki Mo
abstract: Nardostachys jatamansi has traditionally been used to treat gastrointestinal disorders. Although it was recently reported to have anti-inflammatory properties, the pharmacological potential of water extract of Nardostachys jatamansi (WENJ) against atopic dermatitis (AD)-like skin inflammation remains unclear. We investigated the effects of WENJ on a house dust mite-induced AD-like mouse model by assessing phenotypic severity, histopathological changes, and cytokine expression. Transcriptomic analysis of murine skin tissues was performed to identify gene expression signatures and key transcription factors contributing to the efficacy of WENJ. In addition, the role of the primary bioactive component of WENJ, desoxo-narchinol A, was examined in interleukin (IL)-4/IL-13-stimulated human keratinocytes, with a focus on nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2)/heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) signaling. In the AD-like mouse model, oral administration of WENJ markedly alleviated AD-like symptoms, reduced immune cell infiltration and inflammatory mediator expression, and restored the expression of skin barrier proteins such as filaggrin. The Nrf2/HO-1 pathway was identified as a key molecular pathway underlying the effects of WENJ on AD-like skin inflammation. Moreover, desoxo-narchinol A significantly increased Nrf2/HO-1 expression in keratinocytes, and exhibited the ability to bind Keap1 in molecular docking analysis. These findings demonstrate that WENJ and its active constituent desoxo-narchinol A exert anti-inflammatory and skin-protective effects through activation of the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway, highlighting their potential as promising therapeutic candidates for AD and related inflammatory skin conditions.

title: TFXcan reveals transcription factor programs driving GWAS loci.
authors: Adeluwa, Temidayo; Salazar-Magana, Sofia; Sumner, Sarah; Gona, Saideep; Nyasimi, Festus; Carbonetto, Peter; Baca, Sylvan C; Freedman, Matthew; Gusev, Alexander; Liu, Boxiang; Madduri, Ravi; Stephens, Matthew; Gao, Guimin; Amariuta, Tiffany; Im, Hae Kyung
abstract: Disease-associated loci identified by genome-wide association studies (GWASs) may induce effects by altering transcription factor (TF) binding. However, due to the scarcity of population-level TF-binding experiments, identifying these disrupted TFs remains challenging. To address this, we present the TFXcan framework, which correlates genetically predicted TF binding with phenotypes to nominate TF-tissue pairs that may regulate complex traits. Within this framework, we introduce Enpact, a deep learning-based approach that integrates Enformer and IMPACT to infer personalized TF-binding events. Leveraging Enpact, we correlate predicted binding profiles for 700 TF-tissue pairs with prostate cancer risk, identifying multiple implicated TFs at risk loci. Matrix decomposition further reveals clusters of TF-tissue pairs, termed "programs," acting as candidate drivers of disease risk. TFXcan represents the first method capable of predicting TF binding from genotype data at scale, enabling systematic identification of TFs and regulatory programs underlying complex traits.

title: Binding pocket optimization of Pueraria mirifica type II chalcone isomerase synergizing with a necrosis-attenuating host transcription factor for persistent daidzein biosynthesis.
authors: Suntichaikamolkul, Nithiwat; Sanachai, Kamonpan; Nutho, Bodee; Rungrotmongkol, Thanyada; Tubtimrattana, Apinya; Thirati, Parath; Sucharitakul, Jeerus; Sirikantaramas, Supaart
abstract: Pathway reconstitution of leguminous isoflavonoids in non-legume plant chassis offers a tractably controlled environment to probe specialized metabolism, yet it remains critically bottlenecked by suboptimal heterologous enzyme efficiency and severe host tissue necrosis. Here, we overcome these long-standing architectural limitations by establishing a highly synergistic, necrosis-attenuated Nicotiana benthamiana synthetic biology platform. We characterized chalcone isomerases from Pueraria mirifica (PmCHIs), revealing that PmCHI Type II operates as a biochemical junction exhibiting a specialized substrate-dependent alkaline optimum (pH 7.5-8.0) exclusively toward isoliquiritigenin. Combining 500-ns molecular dynamics simulations with structure-guided mutagenesis, active-site engineering identified an I195V variant with enhanced isoliquiritigenin preference. The conservative I195V substitution was predicted to reduce local steric crowding and produced an isoliquiritigenin selectivity ratio of 1.63 in vitro. For in planta pathway integration, we delivered a polycistronic cascade using P2A ribosome-skipping peptides to streamline multiplex multi-gene stacking. Crucially, substituting the conventional Arabidopsis thaliana MYB12 regulator with a host-derived N. benthamiana MYB60 transcription factor successfully attenuated tissue necrosis, accompanied by reduced electrolyte leakage. Quantitative proteomics showed no statistically significant difference in PmCHI abundance between the I195V and WT-II treatments in planta, while independent plant batches consistently showed higher daidzein accumulation with I195V, although the magnitude of enhancement varied among experiments. The NbMYB60-based platform extended the operational viability window up to 9 days, delivering a robust daidzein titer of 1.5 mg/g DW at 6 days post-infiltration, with individual high-performing replicates reaching up to 2.5 mg/g DW. Together, these results establish an integrated enzyme-engineering and necrosis-attenuating regulatory framework for persistent daidzein biosynthesis and specialized pathway reconstitution in planta.

title: An extensible deep learning framework for multi-type chromatin interaction prediction through hierarchical adaptation strategies.
authors: Wang, Shuaibin; Chen, Tong; Liu, Weixu; Zheng, Xuejie; Yang, Zhongxin; Liang, Zhen; Shen, Yin
abstract: Three-dimensional chromatin interactions play essential roles in gene regulation, yet computational prediction of diverse interaction types remains largely dependent on specialized, single-task models. Here, we present UniLoopNet, a multi-task deep learning framework that predicts multiple types of chromatin interactions including enhancer-promoter interactions, enhancer-enhancer interactions, CTCF-mediated loops, and stripe-associated interactions from DNA sequences. UniLoopNet employs a shared encoder-decoder architecture with hierarchical adaptation strategies, integrating multi-task, transfer, and continual learning based on task semantic similarity. Comprehensive benchmarking across multiple cell lines demonstrates that UniLoopNet outperforms existing specialized and multi-task approaches, with AUROCs exceeding 0.90 in most tasks. Under stringent evaluation settings, including chromosome-matched, distance-matched, realistic imbalanced, and locus-disjoint tests, AUROCs range from 0.8934 to 0.9366. In the realistic 1:5 class-imbalance setting, the AUPRCs for enhancer-promoter and enhancer-enhancer interaction prediction are 0.7956 and 0.6935, respectively. Cross-cell-line transfer experiments further show that applying UniLoopNet to another cell line requires adaptation by supervised fine-tuning on target-cell-line data, after which performance is comparable to that of within-cell-line training. Notably, the framework exhibits data efficiency in experiments with substantially reduced training data. Interpretability analyses reveal that the learned sequence features are associated with known transcription factor binding sites and uncover differential regulatory effects of disease-associated variants. UniLoopNet provides a versatile and data-efficient framework for sequence-based prediction and interpretation of diverse 3D genome interactions, complementing existing sequence-to-map approaches while improving the understanding of sequence-encoded regulatory potential.

title: In Silico Investigation of Candidate Anticancer Targets for Aryltetralin Lignans Previously Reported from Cleistanthus Species.
authors: Nguyen, Lam-Hong; Nguyen, Thi-Thanh-Thuy; Nguyen, Dac-Nhan; Mai, Quang-Minh; Le, Thang; Pham-The, Hai; Pham, Van-Cuong; Doan, Thi-Mai-Huong; Tran, Viet-Hung; Thai, Khac-Minh
abstract: Aryltetralin lignans isolated from the fruits of Cleistanthus species exhibit substantial cytotoxic activity, although the molecular interactions underlying these effects remain incompletely understood. This study combined computational target investigation with previously published experimental chemical characterization and cytotoxic evidence and no new isolation or cytotoxicity experiments were carried out. Cleistantoxin, 7-hydroxypicropolygamain, neo-cleistantoxin, cleisindoside A, cleisindoside D, and cleistonkinin D were previously isolated from C. indochinensis, C. tonkinensis, C. eberhardtii and characterized by complementary spectroscopic methods. Cleistantoxin showed potent activity against MCF-7, multidrug-resistant MCF-7R, and HT29 cells, with reported IC(50) values of 0.036, 0.014, and 0.035 muM, respectively. Structural similarity to podophyllotoxin-derived anticancer agents guided the investigation of DNA topoisomerase IIbeta, Bcl-2, and p53 Y220C as candidate targets. Docking with AutoDock Vina-GPU 2.1 was validated by redocking the co-crystallized inhibitors (RMSD < 2 A at the TOP2B and Bcl-2 sites; the p53 Y220C control is reported for both receptor preparations), and selected complexes were simulated in triplicate for 100 ns, followed by MM-GBSA calculations and ADMET predictions. Cleisindoside A and D kept etoposide-like hydrogen bonds to DNA in the TOP2B-DNA complex. Their MM-GBSA binding energies were -78.40 +/- 3.73 and -81.90 +/- 7.84 kcal.mol(-1) for two ligand copies, comparable to -79.62 +/- 5.14 kcal.mol(-1) for etoposide. In Bcl-2, S-10r was clearly more favorable than cleisindoside D. The predicted pharmacokinetic profiles differentiated the aglycones from the glycosides and identified potential cytochrome P450 inhibition liabilities. By linking previously reported experimentally characterized natural products and cytotoxic evidence with molecular modeling, this study provides testable hypotheses for the molecular recognition of Cleistanthus lignans. Direct biochemical and mechanism-focused cellular studies are nevertheless required to validate the proposed targets.

title: Butein Interacts at the Minor Groove of DNA: Multi-Spectroscopic, Thermodynamic, and Bioinformatic Analyses.
authors: Alrehaili, Jihad; Anwer, Razique
abstract: DNA is an important therapeutic target, and characterizing its interactions with small molecules can inform drug development. Butein is a chalcone with reported antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer activities. This study investigated the interaction between butein and calf thymus DNA using spectroscopic and computational methods. UV-visible absorption and fluorescence quenching measurements supported complex formation. Fluorescence-derived binding constants ranged from 4.04 x 10(3) to 5.62 x 10(3) M(-1), indicating weak to moderate binding affinity. Thermodynamic analysis indicated spontaneous binding that was both enthalpically and entropically favourable. DNA melting, urea disruption, viscosity, and competitive displacement assays supported a predominantly minor-groove binding mode. Molecular docking identified hydrogen bonds and van der Waals contacts between butein and DNA. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested that the complex remained stable over 250 ns at 310 K, with limited changes in DNA structure and dynamic hydrogen bonding. These findings characterize the interaction between butein and DNA and provide a basis for further investigation of its biological significance.

title: Targeting FTSJ1 to Restore TP53 Function in Nonsense Mutation-Driven Cancer: Computational and Experimental Evaluation of 1,2,4-Triazole Derivatives.
authors: Roomi, Muhammad Sohaib; Culletta, Giulia; Lombardo, Vincenzo; Vitale, Emanuele; Ricci, Davide; Varrica, Riccardo; Fiduccia, Ignazio; Pace, Andrea; Lentini, Laura; Pibiri, Ivana; Tutone, Marco
abstract: Nonsense mutations introduce premature termination codons (PTCs) into mRNA transcripts, leading to truncated and non-functional proteins, and accounting for approximately 10-15% of genetic disorders. In this context, the induction of translational readthrough by small molecules, known as translational readthrough-inducing drugs (TRIDs), has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy to restore full-length protein expression. However, the mechanism of action of TRIDs is still under debate, and one emerging target is FTSJ1, a methyltransferase involved in tRNA modification. FTSJ1 regulates translational fidelity and nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, and its inhibition has been proposed to facilitate the restoration of full-length proteins from nonsense-mutated genes. In this study, we investigated the inhibition of FTSJ1 methyltransferase by a novel series of TRIDs, the 1,2,4-triazole derivatives IP14, IP15, IP17, and IP18, using a luciferase assay in HeLa cells transfected with the pFLuc190UGA plasmid, which in our previous studies showed the rescue of p53 expression in H1299 R213X cells with TP53 gene harboring the R213X nonsense mutation. An integrated computational workflow, including induced fit docking, binding pose metadynamics, molecular dynamics simulations, and MM-GBSA analysis, was employed to characterize their interaction within the FTSJ1 catalytic pocket. The computational results revealed stable binding modes and favorable energetic profiles, supporting the hypothesis that inhibition of FTSJ1 may contribute to their biological activity. Consistent with these findings, in vitro assays supported their translational readthrough activity, suggesting a possible mechanism of action.

title: Effects of a Benzimidazolium Salt on Colorectal Cancer Cells: Involvement of Apoptosis and Autophagy.
authors: Cakir, Mustafa; Acikgoz, Eda; Kuzu, Burak; Akar, Sakine; Ozkol, Halil; Donmez-Altuntas, Hamiyet; Akkoc, Senem
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, necessitating the identification of novel small molecules capable of targeting multiple survival pathways. In this study, the antiproliferative potential of dds benzimidazole-palladium (Pd) complexes was evaluated across breast cancer (4T1, MDA-MB-231) and CRC (DLD-1, HT-29) cell lines using MTT assays. Following initial screening, CRC models were prioritized for mechanistic investigation due to the complexes' superior cytotoxic profile, particularly that of the lead candidate 3a, which exhibited significant dose-dependent efficacy. Mechanistic analyses, employing immunofluorescence staining for LC3 and mTOR alongside Annexin V/PI flow cytometry, revealed that compound 3a triggers a potent dual response characterized by concomitant autophagy and apoptosis. Furthermore, functional assays indicated that 3a significantly impairs the metastatic hallmarks of CRC cells by inhibiting migration, cell adhesion, and colony formation. Gene expression profiling further elucidated that the anticancer efficacy of 3a is mediated by suppression of the AKT/mTOR/STAT3 signaling axis, thereby triggering an autophagic response that destabilizes cell adhesion and accelerates apoptosis. These molecular findings were corroborated by in silico molecular docking analyses, which demonstrated favorable binding affinities between compound 3a and key regulatory proteins, specifically BCL-2 and Caspase-3. Collectively, these results identify compound 3a as a promising multi-targeted anticancer agent that disrupts critical survival and metastatic pathways in CRC, warranting further preclinical and mechanistic exploration for therapeutic development.

title: Drugging the Undruggable in Oncology: Structural Computation, Machine Learning, and Generative AI for Historically Intractable Targets.
authors: Stanczak, Mikolaj; Niazi, Sarfaraz
abstract: For four decades the central oncogenic drivers of human cancer the RAS GTPases, the transcription-factor MYC, mutant p53, and the protein-tyrosine phosphatases, fusion oncoproteins and intrinsically disordered regulators that surround them were regarded as undruggable: lacking deep, well-defined small-molecule binding pockets, governed by femtomolar substrate affinities, or driven through flat protein-protein interfaces that classical medicinal chemistry could not engage. The last decade has overturned that verdict. This narrative review argues that the convergence of three advances has made the undruggable proteome systematically approachable: the discovery of cryptic, allosteric and induced pockets through molecular dynamics and deep learning; the maturation of physics-based and machine-learned models that can read out binding from structure; and the rise in generative artificial intelligence that can design novel molecules conditioned directly on a three-dimensional target. We develop the argument in full formal detail. We set out the mathematics of modern molecular machine learning E(3)/SE(3)-equivariant graph neural networks, denoising diffusion and score-based generative models, and generative flow networks alongside the statistical mechanics of binding free energy (free-energy perturbation, thermodynamic integration, MM-PBSA), the kinetics of covalent inhibition, the equilibrium theory of ternary complexes and cooperativity that governs molecular glues and degraders, and the pharmacology that determines whether a designed molecule reaches and acts on a tumour. We then examine, target by target, the biology that made each oncoprotein intractable and the campaigns structural, chemical and increasingly computational that have begun to defeat it, distinguishing throughout what classical structural and computational work achieved, what machine learning demonstrably contributed, and what generative design has so far only promised: the switch-II pocket and the covalent KRAS-G12C and non-covalent KRAS-G12D and pan-RAS(ON) inhibitors; the mutation-created cavity of p53-Y220C and its first reactivators; the disordered MYC-MAX interface and the miniprotein Omomyc; and the allosteric tunnel of SHP2. These four are selected for mechanistic non-redundancy, on grounds we state explicitly, and the structured search framework and eligibility criteria underlying the review are documented. We foreground the newest evidence AlphaFold3, RoseTTAFold All-Atom, deep cryptic-pocket predictors, and the first generative-to-clinic existence proofs while maintaining candour about the field's hard limits: the physical-validity and generalisation gaps of deep docking, the bounded accuracy and cost of free-energy methods, the synthesizability gap, dual-use risk, and a clinical attrition that artificial intelligence has not yet reduced. The synthesis we offer is not that the problem is solved but that it has changed in kind: from a search for the rare tractable target to the deliberate, computable engineering of molecules against targets once thought beyond reach.

title: Developmental and Regulatory Framework of Shoot Branching in Plants.
authors: Yue, Linan; Liu, Shuo; Yu, Song
abstract: How do plants build a branch? Shoot branching is a fundamental determinant of plant architecture and is best understood as a dynamic developmental program governed by the coordinated action of multiple regulatory processes rather than by isolated pathways. Branch formation proceeds through a series of coordinated developmental transitions, from axillary meristem initiation and bud establishment to dormancy, activation, and sustained branch outgrowth, driven by interactions among phytohormones, transcription factors, environmental cues, and cellular processes. Here, we propose a developmental framework that integrates these successive stages and synthesize recent advances from both herbaceous and woody plants to illustrate how hormonal, transcriptional, and environmental signals coordinate branch development. We further highlight that these regulatory networks ultimately converge on fundamental cellular processes-including cell cycle progression, vascular differentiation, cell wall remodeling, and mechanical regulation-to execute branch formation. Finally, we discuss the evolutionary diversification of branching mechanisms and emerging technologies, including single-cell and spatial omics, comparative genomics, and artificial intelligence, that are advancing our understanding of shoot branching and accelerating the molecular design of plant architecture. This review provides an integrated framework for understanding how plants build branches and offers new perspectives for future research and crop improvement.

title: M4-like Macrophages Drive Skeletal Muscle Fibrosis and Suppress Myogenesis via the MMP12/SPP1/NF-kappaB Axis.
authors: Yao, Senwen; Lu, Zhenyuan; Zhao, Guosheng; Liu, Yang; Wu, Shan; Zhang, Jiaxuan; Dong, Renjie; Hu, Yangming; Zhang, Ye; Wang, Yang
abstract: Acute skeletal muscle repair depends on a finely tuned balance between myogenic regeneration and fibrotic remodeling. Macrophages are essential to this process, and specific subsets have been linked to fibrosis in some organs. The M4-like macrophage, a distinct polarization subset implicated in fibrotic diseases, has not been well characterized in the context of injured muscle, particularly regarding its impact on fibroblast activation and myogenic suppression. The study aims to explore the effects of M4-like macrophages in the repair of muscle injury and possible mechanism. We analyzed a murine single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset from cardiotoxin (CTX)-injured skeletal muscle to identify injury-expanded macrophage subsets and their molecular programs. Immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence staining of muscle sections were used to assess CXCL4 expression and platelet (CD41(+)) infiltration in injured versus uninjured tissues. CXCL4-induced M4-like macrophages were established as an in vitro model to examine their effects on L929 fibroblasts and C2C12 myoblasts. The MMP12-SPP1 interaction was predicted by AlphaFold3 and validated by co-immunoprecipitation and immunofluorescence colocalization. Loss-of-function and rescue experiments targeting MMP12 and SPP1 were performed to determine their causal roles in fibroblast activation and myogenic suppression. Transcriptomic and biochemical analyses were used to define downstream macrophage-intrinsic NF-kappaB/TNF-alpha signaling. Finally, AAV-mediated macrophage-targeted SPP1 knockdown and pharmacological NF-kappaB inhibition were evaluated in the CTX injury model. Using a BALB/c mouse model of cardiotoxin (CTX)-induced acute skeletal muscle injury and a publicly available murine scRNA-seq dataset from CTX-injured skeletal muscle, we observed an injury-induced MMP12/SPP1-positive macrophage subset with an M4-like transcriptional signature. Mechanistically, co-immunoprecipitation assays and immunofluorescence colocalization supported an association between MMP12 and SPP1. MMP12 knockdown attenuated the pro-fibrotic and anti-myogenic effects of M4-like macrophages, whereas recombinant SPP1 largely restored these phenotypes. Furthermore, transcriptomic and biochemical analyses revealed that autocrine SPP1 activated NF-kappaB signaling in M4-like macrophages, and increased TNF-alpha secretion. Pharmacological inhibition of NF-kappaB signaling with QNZ reduced fibroblast activation and restored the expression of myogenic markers. However, QNZ is not TNF-alpha specific and may affect multiple cell types. In vivo, AAV-mediated macrophage-targeted SPP1 knockdown driven by the F4/80 promoter, as well as QNZ treatment in the CTX-induced muscle injury model, markedly decreased collagen deposition, enhanced myogenic regeneration, and improved functional recovery. These findings identify an MMP12/SPP1/NF-kappaB signaling pathway in M4-like macrophages, with TNF-alpha as a potential downstream mediator, that may contribute to an imbalance between regeneration and fibrosis and may represent a therapeutic target for enhancing skeletal muscle repair after acute injury.

title: Fenvalerate Induces Airway Epithelial Injury Through CHRM3-Associated NF-kappaB Activation.
authors: Yang, Yuxin; Li, Jixin; Liu, Tong; Sheng, Mingyang; Liu, Jiatong; Yang, Zidong; Chu, Hongbo; Jia, Ailing; Xu, Wei
abstract: Fenvalerate (FEN) is a widely used pyrethroid insecticide with potential respiratory toxicity; however, its contribution to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)-related pathological processes remains unclear. We investigated molecular mechanisms linking FEN exposure to airway epithelial injury. COPD transcriptomic datasets were integrated with predicted FEN targets, and candidate genes were prioritized using machine-learning algorithms. Immune infiltration and single-cell transcriptomic analyses were used to examine immune associations and cell-type-specific expression. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations assessed potential FEN-target interactions, followed by validation in BEAS-2B human bronchial epithelial cells. Intersecting FEN-COPD genes were enriched in inflammatory, immune-regulatory, neuroactive ligand-receptor, and epithelial injury-related pathways. Eight candidate genes showed distinct expression patterns across airway epithelial and immune cell populations. Computational analyses supported a potentially stable FEN-CHRM3 interaction. In BEAS-2B cells, FEN reduced viability, increased IL-6 and IL-8 secretion, promoted apoptosis, upregulated CHRM3, and enhanced IkappaBalpha and p65 phosphorylation. Pharmacological inhibition of CHRM3 or NF-kappaB partially attenuated these responses. Thus, FEN-induced epithelial inflammation and apoptosis may involve CHRM3-associated NF-kappaB activation, providing mechanistic insight into pesticide-related respiratory toxicity.

title: Novel Genetic Variants of the CHD2 Gene in cis Position in a Patient with Epileptic Encephalopathy: A Case Report and In Silico Analysis of the Impact of the Variants on the Protein.
authors: Zuev, Andrew S; Fonova, Elizaveta A; Kuznetsova, Daria S; Stepanov, Vadim A; Skryabin, Nikolay A
abstract: CHD2-related neurodevelopmental disorders are increasingly recognized as a distinct group of epileptic encephalopathies with heterogeneous clinical manifestations. Here, we report a 12-year-old female patient with pharmacoresistant epilepsy, mild cognitive impairment (IQ = 56), and extraneurological features including grade II kyphoscoliosis and planovalgus foot deformity. Video-EEG monitoring revealed a phenotype consistent with Jeavons syndrome, characterized by daily eyelid myoclonia with absences and marked photosensitivity with an eye closure sensitivity (ECS) phenomenon. Molecular genetic testing via whole-exome and Sanger sequencing identified two novel variants in the CHD2 gene (NM_001271.4): c.1634T>G (p.Leu545Arg) and c.3810G>C (p.Leu1270Phe). Long-read nanopore sequencing confirmed their de novo status and cis-positioning on the paternal allele. Structural bioinformatic analysis using AlphaFold3, FoldX/mCSM (v5.0 package), UCSF ChimeraX (v1.10.1), and PyMOL (v3.1.8) demonstrated that both variants individually destabilize the CHD2 protein, with a cumulative destabilizing effect when combined: p.Leu545Arg affects the ATP-binding domain, whereas p.Leu1270Phe disrupts hydrophobic packing within the C-terminal DNA-binding domain. These findings suggest accelerated protein degradation as a potential disease mechanism. Our data support the pathogenicity of these heterozygous cis-variants and implicate CHD2 haploinsufficiency as the leading etiopathogenic mechanism, though distinct domain-specific effects of each substitution may also contribute to the complex molecular synergy observed in this case.

title: Pyrazolate-Bridged PdCo and PdCu Complexes as Dual DNA-Binding and ROS-Driven Cytotoxic Agents.
authors: Uvarova, Marina A; Kulikova, Vitalia V; Kozmenko, Yaroslav V; Revtovich, Svetlana V; Filippova, Arina D; Shmelev, Maxim A; Sokolova, Darina V; Pokrovsky, Vadim S; Kaverina, Alexandra P; Solyev, Pavel N; Eremenko, Igor L
abstract: Heterometallic complexes offer a promising anticancer strategy owing to their simultaneous action on multiple biological targets. In this work, we report the synthesis and evaluation of the antitumor potential of two heterometallic pyrazolate-bridged complexes, [PdCo(phen)(micro-dmpz)(2)(OOCMe)(2)] (PdCo) and [PdCu(phen)(micro-dmpz)(2)(OOCMe)(2)] (PdCu) (phen = 1,10-phenanthroline, dmpz = 3,5-dimethylpyrazole). The complexes were comprehensively characterized using a combined spectroscopic and analytical approach, including single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SC-XRD), PXRD, FTIR, UV-Vis, and mass spectrometry, confirming their structural integrity in both solid state and solution. Their cytotoxicity was assessed in vitro against colon, A549 lung, and breast cancer cell lines, as well as normal human dermal fibroblasts. The complexes exhibited micromolar IC(50) values with selectivity indices up to 7. Using circular dichroism (CD) and fluorescence spectroscopy, it was demonstrated that PdCo binds to DNA, with minor groove binding (K(d) = 7.6 muM) being the preferred mode of interaction, dominating over intercalation (K(d) = 26.1 muM). Molecular docking simulations confirmed that the dissociated [Pd(phen)(micro-dmpz)(2)] fragment is capable of binding to DNA. Furthermore, chemiluminescence assays revealed pronounced peroxidase-like and superoxide dismutase-like activities of PdCu and PdCo, implicating ROS-mediated oxidative stress as a second, complementary cytotoxic pathway. Collectively, these findings highlight the dual-action mechanism of the synthesized complexes, combining DNA targeting with ROS-mediated oxidative damage, positioning them as highly potent candidates for further anticancer development.

title: Integrative Bioinformatics Analysis Incorporating Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Identifies Putative Pathogenic HNF1B Missense Variants Associated with HNF1B-MODY.
authors: Aldharee, Hitham
abstract: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 5 (MODY5 or HNF1B-MODY) is a rare form of diabetes caused by variants in HNF1B. Patients with MODY5 exhibit high blood sugar levels and symptoms commonly associated with both type 1 and type 2 diabetes (T1D, T2D), along with kidney and pancreatic issues. Nonetheless, diagnosis, treatment and management approaches depend on specific genotype-phenotype associations. Interpretation of HNF1B missense variants remains challenging because of conflicting classifications and limited clinical evidence. This study aimed to improve the interpretation of HNF1B missense variants with conflicting evidence regarding pathogenicity and thereby advance the genetic and molecular understanding of HNF1B-MODY. An integrative computational approach combining artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and conventional bioinformatic tools, including Panther, SIFT, SNAP2, Meta-SNP, PhD-SNP, PolyPhen-2, and AlphaMissense, was used to identify deleterious missense variants in the HNF1B gene. The variants were further processed to determine their effects on protein conformation, stability, function, and conservation across species. Among 982 reported variants retrieved from the ClinVar database, 368 were classified as missense. Only 47 missense variants were labelled with conflicting classification and reported with clinical uncertainty. Consensus analysis by all tools identified five candidate variants (His153Arg, Asn298Asp, Arg303His, Lys305Glu, and Val458Gly), representing 10.6% (5/47) as potentially pathogenic. AlphaMissense classified all five as likely pathogenic, with scores ranging from 0.8921 to 1.000. Secondary structure analysis indicates that the His153Arg, Asn298Asp, Arg303His, and Lys305Glu variants are in the helical region, while the Val458Gly variant is located within the coil region. Interestingly, all five filtered variants are predicted by the I-Mutant and MuPro tools to reduce protein stability. The three-dimensional (3D) protein structures were constructed using the Deep Learning-Based Iterative Threading Assembly Refinement (D-I-TASSER) tool and visualised by UCSF Chimera. Structural modelling showed similarity between the mutant and wild-type models, with RMSD values ranging from 0.77 to 1.36 A. The multiple sequence alignments show that amino acids at variant sites across all variants are highly conserved among species. These findings show that combining traditional bioinformatics with artificial intelligence and machine learning improves the interpretation of HNF1B missense variants with clinical uncertainty. Integrating computational predictions with structural, evolutionary, and clinical data provides a framework for prioritising variants for further functional and clinical investigation.

title: Identification of Genes Associated with Gut Microbiota Metabolites in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Complicated by Acute Cerebral Infarction Based on Bioinformatics and Mendelian Randomization.
authors: Zhang, Guimei; Ju, Jiasheng; Zhang, Run; Xu, Xiuyuan; Li, Lifeng; Zhao, Jing; Ju, Haibing
abstract: Background: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and acute cerebral infarction (ACI) are globally prevalent diseases that impose substantial public health burdens. While gut microbiota (GM) is increasingly recognized to regulate metabolic and immune homeostasis linked to both diseases, its shared genetically predicted microbial taxa and underlying metabolite-gene regulatory mechanisms in T2DM and ACI remain unclear, highlighting the need for systematic investigation. Accordingly, this study aimed to elucidate their regulatory mechanisms. Methods: Transcriptomic datasets, genome-wide association study (GWAS) data, and GM data were retrieved from public databases. Key microbial taxa were identified using two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) and 16S rRNA sequencing. Metabolite-target genes (MTGs) were predicted via public databases. Key metabolites were screened based on Lipinski's rules and low toxicity, and key genes were prioritized by molecular docking. Regulatory networks and potential drugs were predicted using public databases. Results: Using the FinnGen diabetes endpoint as a proxy for T2DM-related genetic susceptibility, MR analysis identified 12 candidate microbial taxa shared by both diseases. Further intersection with the top 30 microbial taxa from 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed two key microbial taxa (Alistipes and Bifidobacterium). Subsequently, 602 MTGs were identified for metabolites derived from the key microbial taxa. After druggability evaluation and toxicity profiling, nine key metabolites with favorable druggability and low toxicity were identified. Molecular docking predicted binding affinities between these key metabolites and the encoded proteins, suggesting ANPEP and CYP1B1 as candidate key genes. Additionally, ANPEP interacted with 12 transcription factors (TFs), while CYP1B1 was regulated by six TFs and 13 microRNAs that further interacted with 26 long noncoding RNAs. Sixty-eight and 32 potential drugs targeting ANPEP and CYP1B1, respectively, were identified, providing candidates for translational research. Conclusion: This study systematically identified ANPEP and CYP1B1 as candidate key genes in the GM-associated regulatory network underlying T2DM-related genetic susceptibility and ACI, providing candidate molecular targets and candidate compounds for the development of GM-based targeted therapies.

title: Donor-Resolved Analysis of HES1-Associated Fibroblast States in Systemic Sclerosis.
authors: Fang, Shenyi; Huang, Lin; Wang, Mingzhu
abstract: Background/Objectives: We examined HES1-associated fibroblast states in systemic sclerosis (SSc) and the rationale for testing upstream gamma-secretase inhibition with nirogacestat. Methods: We analysed 325,636 skin cells from 230 donors across five non-redundant cohorts using complete computational transcription-factor screens, donor-level activity and trajectory analyses, multiome data and spatial assays. Donors or independent simulations were the inference units, with cohort adjustment and multiplicity correction where applicable. Three independent 200 ns molecular dynamics runs per condition compared nirogacestat-bound and ligand-deleted gamma-secretase models. Results: HES1 activity was positively associated with model-derived myofibroblast fate in 98.1% of 206 donors (median Spearman's rho=0.282; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.258-0.309). The adjusted SSc-healthy control activity difference was uncertain (0.21; 95% CI, -0.01 to 0.43; Benjamini-Hochberg q=0.061). HES1 ranked 28/107 and 30/109 in the descriptive screens; SMAD3 showed a stronger association with cell fate. Disease-specific communication and contact-enrichment tests did not provide statistical support. The adjusted Visium association was negative; Xenium showed a weak positive mean without section-level corrected support. Nirogacestat was selected retrospectively through mechanistic and translational evidence despite a weak expression-reversal signal and discordant tofacitinib-signature alignment. Simulations showed lower reference-defined pocket root mean square deviation (RMSD) in bound models, with substantial sampling and endpoint-energy uncertainty. Conclusions: HES1 activity marks a consistent fibroblast-state association, with uncertain causality and SSc specificity. Nirogacestat is a candidate compound for experimental testing of upstream Notch-pathway perturbation in SSc fibroblasts; the computational findings do not establish efficacy.

title: Integrative Multi-Omics and Machine Learning Unveil Plakophilin 1 as a Robust Diagnostic Biomarker for Thymoma.
authors: Li, Yunhan; Zhang, Shen; Gao, Qian; Ding, Shanshan; Sun, Mengling; Xue, Haiying; Yang, Fan; Liu, Yangyang; An, Xiaokang; Dong, Xiaotao; Zhang, Guoyu
abstract: Background: Thymoma (THYM) is a rare epithelial tumor originating in the anterior mediastinum. Due to the lack of specific clinical manifestations and reliable molecular biomarkers, its diagnosis and treatment are often delayed until advanced stages. Although multi-omics technologies have provided new strategies for biomarker discovery, systematic integrative studies specifically focused on thymoma remain limited. Objectives: This study aimed to identify and validate potential diagnostic biomarkers for thymoma through the integration of multi-omics data and machine learning approaches. Methods: We integrated transcriptomic, proteomic, and epigenomic datasets and applied machine learning algorithms to screen for core candidate genes. The cell-type-specific expression patterns of the identified candidates were further evaluated using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and their potential molecular functions were predicted via in silico perturbation analysis. In addition, immunohistochemistry (IHC) was performed to validate the differential expression of the candidate biomarker at the protein level. Results: Six core candidate genes-interferon regulatory factor 6 (IRF6), thyroid hormone receptor interactor 6 (TRIP6), plakophilin 1 (PKP1), cadherin 1 (CDH1), pre-B-cell leukemia transcription factor 1 (PBX1), and keratin 1 (KRT1)-were identified through machine learning. Among these, PKP1 demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance in both the training set (area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, AUC: 0.83; sensitivity: 0.80; specificity: 0.875) and the validation set (AUC: 0.94; sensitivity: 0.93; specificity: 1.000). Single-cell RNA sequencing confirmed a significantly enriched expression pattern of PKP1 in thymoma tumor cells. In silico perturbation analysis suggested that PKP1 may be involved in cell adhesion and tumor progression through regulation of the extracellular matrix (ECM)-integrin-cytoskeleton axis.
